name: Ming dynasty

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 3,655,000 km2 for 1600 (low); the world_1600 polygon measures ~5.97 million km2 (high) because it takes in loosely held Liaodong frontier and southwestern tusi lands.

population.note: Late-Ming estimates run 160-200 million (Fairbank and Goldman; Ebrey, via the article; infobox 160M for 1600). Seshat codes 90-110M for 1600 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/269) and OWID/HYDE 98M (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true). Mid is a compromise; registers undercounted heavily.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Beijing ~706,000 in 1600 (Seshat), Jiangnan commercial towns booming.

activePersonnel.note: 16th-century registers listed 3 million hereditary soldiers but contemporary observers counted ~845,000 actual troops (Swope 2009 pp. 19-20, via the article). By the 1570s the army was largely mercenary (Lorge 2011 p. 167).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Registered military households not under arms, local militia (minbing) and tusi native troops; the 1600 Bozhou campaign drew heavily on tusi levies.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Coastal fleet crews, gunners, transport and depot personnel within the 845,000.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Military households were ~20% of households (Swope via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Ming_dynasty) but most were farmers; actual raising capacity limited by silver.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Field armies of hired troops: southern infantry drilled on Qi Jiguang's model with arquebuses, folangji and pikes; 48,000 went to Korea in 1592-93 and 75,000-80,000 in 1597-98 (Swope, Hawley via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War).

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: drilled mercenaries of the frontier and southern armies.

count.note: Educated guess. Hereditary wei-suo garrison soldiers, many far below nominal strength.

training.note: Rubric 0.25: some provinces at 2% of nominal strength by 1587; 60 pirates roamed Nanjing for three months (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Ming_dynasty).

count.note: Educated guess. Housemen (jiading) retinues of frontier generals such as Li Rusong, the elite mounted core.
Contemporary observers counted only ~30,000 cavalry in the 16th-century army (Swope 2009 via the article) (low); Mongol horsemen in generals' retinues and Liaodong horse (educated scaling).
Educated guess. Folangji, great-general guns and other field pieces with field armies and on the northern frontier; very large numbers of small pieces excluded.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Portuguese-derived breech-loaders; Ming guns outranged Japanese at Pyongyang 1593.

count.note: Educated guess. Large war junks (fuchuan, guangchuan) of the Fujian, Zhejiang and Guangdong coastal commands; Chen Lin's squadron fought at Noryang 1598.
Educated guess. Every coastal guard battalion was allotted 50 ships (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Ming_dynasty), most under strength by 1600.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: capable field generals (Li Rusong, Liu Ting) won the Three Great Campaigns, but civil-military friction and eunuch interference hampered command (Swope).

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: mercenary armies loyal to their generals; desertion and arrears in pay.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: Ordos, Korea and Bozhou won, but at ruinous cost.

weapons.note: Anchor 5 (1600): arquebuses, folangji breech-loaders, rockets, grenades.

armor.note: Anchor 4-5: brigandine and lamellar, iron helmets.

ships.note: Anchor 4-5: gun-armed war junks, no galleon-type warships.

fortification.note: Anchor 5 minus: brick-faced Great Wall rebuilt in the 16th century, massive city walls, no bastions.

logistics.note: Anchor 5: Grand Canal, state granaries, silver-financed purchase; 17 million liang of silver and supplies went to Korea (Swope 2009 p. 8 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War).

isr.note: Anchor 4-5: beacon towers on the northern frontier, spies.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 China 1600 = 1,217 (2011 int$); range is the usual uncertainty of the series.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Military costs (frontier silver, the three campaigns) were the largest item in a low-tax state; low = peacetime.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Silk and cotton textiles, porcelain, iron, shipbuilding; silver monetisation.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Jiangnan rice surplus shipped north on the Grand Canal.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Courier roads and the Grand Canal towpath.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Guangzhou, Yuegang, Quanzhou, Fuzhou, Ningbo, Dengzhou, Tianjin.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Private junk trade legalised at Yuegang in 1567; no aggregate figures.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Ming armies in Korea depended on supply through Liaodong and Korean granaries.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Oxen, water buffalo, horses, mules.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: walled cities and depth; rebellions and unpaid garrisons reduce support.

notes: Snapshot = 1600, Wanli reign, at the end of the Three Great Campaigns (Ordos 1592, Korea 1592-98, Bozhou 1599-1600). Personnel convention: the ~845,000 troops actually under arms (mostly hired) are activePersonnel; the 3 million registered hereditary soldiers not serving, militia and tusi levies are trainedReserves. Army figures come from Swope (A Dragon's Head and a Serpent's Tail, 2009) and Lorge via the Military of the Ming dynasty and Imjin War articles; the split into roles is an educated reading. Population convention: provinces and frontier commands of the Ming; Korea and tributary states excluded.
